The '''Minakshisundaram–Pleijel zeta function''' is a [[Zeta function (operator)|zeta function]] encoding the eigenvalues of the [[Laplace operator|Laplacian]] of a [[compact space|compact]] [[Riemannian manifold]]. It was  introduced by {{harvs|txt|author1-link=Subbaramiah Minakshisundaram |first1=Subbaramiah |last1=Minakshisundaram |author2-link=Åke Pleijel| first2=Åke |last2=Pleijel|year=1949}}. The case of a compact region of the plane was treated earlier by {{harvs|txt|last=Carleman|first=Torsten|year=1935}}.

==Definition==

For a compact Riemannian manifold ''M'' of dimension ''N'' with eigenvalues 
<math>\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots </math>  of the [[Laplace–Beltrami operator]] <math>\Delta</math>, the zeta function is given for <math>\operatorname{Re}(s)</math> sufficiently large by

:<math> Z(s) = \mbox{Tr}(\Delta^{-s}) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \vert \lambda_{n} \vert^{-s}.</math>

(where if an eigenvalue is zero it is omitted in the sum). The manifold may have a boundary, in which case one has to prescribe suitable boundary conditions, such as [[Dirichlet boundary condition|Dirichlet]] or [[Neumann boundary condition]]s.

More generally one can define

:<math> Z(P, Q, s) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{f_n(P)f_n(Q)}{ \lambda_{n}^s}</math>

for ''P'' and ''Q'' on the manifold, where the <math>f_n</math> are normalized eigenfunctions. This can be analytically continued to a [[meromorphic function]] of ''s'' for all complex ''s'', and is holomorphic for <math>P\ne Q</math>.

The only possible poles are simple poles at the points <math>s = N/2, N/2-1, N/2-2,\dots, 1/2,-1/2, -3/2,\dots</math> for ''N'' odd, and  at the points <math>s = N/2, N/2-1, N/2-2, \dots,2, 1 </math> for ''N'' even. If ''N'' is odd then <math>Z(P,P,s)</math> vanishes at <math>s= 0, -1, -2,\dots</math>.  If ''N'' is even, the residues at the poles can be explicitly found in terms of the metric, and by the [[Wiener–Ikehara theorem]] we find as a corollary the relation

:<math>\sum_{\lambda_n < T} f_n(P)^2 \sim\frac{T^{N/2}}{(2\sqrt{\pi})^N\Gamma(N/2+1)} </math>,

where the symbol <math>\sim</math> indicates that the quotient of both the sides tend to 1 when T tends to <math>+\infty</math>.<ref>{{cite journal | author1-link=Subbaramiah Minakshisundaram | first1=Subbaramiah | last1=Minakshisundaram | author2-link=Åke Pleijel | first2=Åke | last2=Pleijel | title=Some properties of the eigenfunctions of the Laplace-operator on Riemannian manifolds | doi=10.4153/CJM-1949-021-5 | mr=0031145 | year=1949 | journal=[[Canadian Journal of Mathematics]] | issn=0008-414X | volume=1 | issue=3 | pages=242–256 | doi-access=free }}</ref>
 
The function <math>Z(s)</math> can be recovered from <math>Z(P,P,s)</math> by integrating over the whole manifold ''M'':
:<math>\displaystyle Z(s) = \int_M Z(P,P,s)dP</math>.

==Heat kernel==

The [[analytic continuation]] of the zeta function can be found by expressing it in terms of the [[heat kernel]] 
:<math> K(P,Q,t) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} f_n(P)f_n(Q) e^{- \lambda_{n}t} </math>

as the [[Mellin transform]]
:<math> Z(P,Q,s) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(s)} \int_0^\infty K(P,Q,t) t^{s-1} dt </math>

In particular, we have 
:<math> Z(s) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(s)} \int_0^\infty K(t) t^{s-1} dt </math>

where 
:<math> K(t)=\int_M K(P,P,t)dP=\sum^\infty_{i=1}e^{-\lambda_i t} </math>
is the trace of the heat kernel.

The poles of the zeta function can be found from the asymptotic behavior of the heat kernel as ''t''→0.

==Example==

If the manifold is a circle of dimension ''N''=1, then the eigenvalues of the Laplacian are ''n''<sup>2</sup> for integers ''n''. The zeta function
:<math>Z(s) = \sum_{n\ne 0}\frac{1}{(n^2)^s} = 2\zeta(2s)</math>
where ζ is the [[Riemann zeta function]].

==Applications==

Apply the method of heat kernel to [[asymptotic expansion]] for Riemannian manifold (M,g) we obtain the two following theorems. Both are the resolutions of the [[inverse problem]] in which we get the geometric properties or quantities from spectra of the operators. 

{{ordered list
| 1 = Minakshisundaram–Pleijel Asymptotic Expansion

Let (M,g) be an ''n''-dimensional Riemannian manifold. Then, as ''t''→0+, the trace of the heat kernel has an asymptotic expansion of the form:
<math display="block"> K(t)\sim(4\pi t)^{-n/2}\sum^\infty_{m=0}a_m t^m. </math>
In dim=2, this means that the integral of [[scalar curvature]] tells us the [[Euler characteristic]] of M, by the [[Gauss–Bonnet theorem]].

In particular, 
<math display="block"> a_0=\operatorname{Vol}(M,g),\ \ \ \ a_1=\frac{1}{6}\int_MS(x)dV </math>
where S(x) is scalar curvature, the trace of the [[Ricci curvature]], on M.

| 2 = Weyl Asymptotic Formula
Let M be a compact Riemannian manifold, with eigenvalues
<math> 0=\lambda_0\le\lambda_1\le\lambda_2\cdots, </math>
with each distinct eigenvalue repeated with its multiplicity. Define N(λ) to be the number of eigenvalues less than or equal to <math>\lambda</math>, and let <math>\omega_n</math> denote the volume of the [[unit disk]] in <math>\R^n</math>. Then
<math display="block">N(\lambda)\sim\frac{\omega_n \operatorname{Vol}(M)\lambda^{n/2}}{(2\pi)^n},</math>
as <math>\lambda \to \infty</math>. Additionally, as <math>k \to \infty</math>, 
<math display="block"> (\lambda_k)^{n/2}\sim\frac{(2\pi)^nk}{\omega_n \operatorname{Vol}(M)}.</math>
This is also called [[Weyl's law]], refined from the Minakshisundaram–Pleijel asymptotic expansion.
}}
